title: What makes a practice worth more
summary: How buyers put a price on a small practice, why this one is worth about $650,000 today, and the two-to-three-year work that could roughly double it.

blocks.text: A buyer pays for cash the practice will produce in the future that the buyer can keep without you. Every question in a sale comes back to those three tests: how much cash, how certain, and how dependent on the seller.

That is why two practices with the same revenue sell for very different prices, and why the price of a one-physician practice often surprises its owner. Much of what the practice earns is really the owner's wage for seeing patients. A buyer has to pay someone that wage after you leave.

blocks.title: Price is earnings times a multiple
blocks.text: Earnings measure how much cash. The multiple measures how certain it is and how well it transfers. You raise the price by raising either one, and the multiple is usually the cheaper one to move.

blocks.text: EBITDA means earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. It is a rough measure of cash produced by operations, before financing and tax choices.

blocks.title: Two kinds of earnings, two kinds of multiple
blocks.text: Owner earnings (also called seller's discretionary earnings) are measured before any owner pay. EBITDA is measured after a market wage. A multiple of one cannot be applied to the other. Mixing them is the most common way owners overestimate value.

blocks.q: A practice earns $500,000 before paying its only physician. Market pay for that work is $350,000. A buyer offers 4 times EBITDA. What is the offer?
blocks.why: EBITDA is $500,000 minus $350,000, which is $150,000. Four times that is $600,000. The $2,000,000 answer applies an EBITDA multiple to owner earnings.

blocks.text: Normalizing means restating earnings as a new owner would experience them.

rows: Less collections estimated as one-time recovery of old receivables
Less a market wage for the physician's work, with payroll tax and benefits
blocks.caption: Market wage: $325,000 base. Published 2025 figures run from $304,411 (geriatrics average, Doximity) to $342,411 (family medicine median, AMGA).

blocks.text: Then the multiple. The published band for small primary care is 3 to 6 times. This practice sits in the lower half: one physician, government fee-for-service payers, and facility relationships it does not own. A planning range of 2 to 4 times gives $340,000 to $680,000. Cross-checks on owner earnings and on revenue come out higher, $630,000 to $940,000. Weighting them gives about **$650,000**, within a range of $400,000 to $1,000,000.

blocks.text: Buyers check coding themselves. Medicare publishes every clinician's code counts each year, so a buyer's analyst can see this practice's level mix before the first meeting. An unexplained outlier becomes a lower price, money held back in escrow, or no deal. The same pattern explained by a clean independent audit becomes a selling point.

sections.heading: Personal goodwill and the key-person problem

blocks.text: Goodwill is the part of the price above tangible assets. It comes in two kinds. Enterprise goodwill belongs to the business: its name, contracts, staff, systems and data. Personal goodwill belongs to you: your reputation and your relationships with administrators, case managers and families.

In a facility-based practice the main asset is the relationship with each facility, and that relationship usually cannot be assigned without the facility's consent. If you retire at closing, a buyer has little reason to pay for goodwill that walks out with you.

items: Buyers handle this with a lower price, an earn-out paid only if revenue holds, and a required period of continued employment.
You handle it by making relationships and methods belong to the practice: a second clinician known at every site, written facility agreements, documented procedures, a team that runs without you.

Tax can favor selling personal goodwill separately, at capital gain rates, but only if you have no existing non-compete or employment agreement with your own corporation. Ask a tax adviser before signing anything with the practice entity.

blocks.text: Price and your pay after the sale move in opposite directions. A buyer that pays more up front will pay you less as an employee, because the price was calculated on earnings left after your wage.

sections.heading: Deal mechanics you should know before the first conversation

items: Most practice sales are asset sales. The buyer gets a tax benefit and avoids unknown liabilities. Sellers generally prefer a stock sale.
You keep the cash and repay the debt. The price is for the business.
In small sales the seller keeps them and collects them.
Both sides report how the price is split among equipment, covenants and goodwill on the same tax form. Goodwill is generally capital gain to the seller. An S corporation pays one level of tax.
Part of the price is held back to cover billing liabilities that surface later. Medicare can look back six years.
Florida enforces reasonable covenants. For the seller of a practice, up to three years is presumed reasonable.
Billing privileges cannot be sold. A change of ownership must be reported within 30 days, a new tax ID needs a new enrollment, and Florida Medicaid wants notice 60 days before.

blocks.q: Why does a buyer hold part of the price in escrow?
choices: To cover billing liabilities that appear after closing
blocks.why: Claims paid before the sale can be reviewed for six years. Escrow is how a buyer protects itself. A clean independent audit is how a seller shrinks it.

sections.heading: A three-year plan to raise the number

rows: Attorney-directed review of care management, visit levels and place of service. Refund what must be refunded.
Removes the largest discount and the largest reason to walk away
Monthly statements. Contracts in one file. Receivables cleaned. Shareholder loan cleared. Expensive debt refinanced.
A second nurse practitioner. Visits shifted from the owner. Written agreements and time logs for medical directorships.
Two years of growth on clean numbers. A formal appraisal. Conversations with more than one type of buyer.
A higher multiple on higher earnings

blocks.text: As an illustration, not a forecast: revenue of $1.4 million with $330,000 of normalized earnings, valued at 4 to 5 times, would be worth about **$1.3 to $1.6 million**. Each additional $100,000 of sustainable earnings is worth roughly $300,000 at today's multiple, and each full turn of the multiple is worth about $170,000 at today's earnings.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text: Selling at the bottom of a revenue decline. Claiming add-backs with no documentation. Letting the buyer discover a billing problem. Signing a non-compete with your own corporation before understanding the tax effect. Starting the tax and entity review after the letter of intent.

takeaways: Buyers pay for future cash they can keep without you: how much, how certain, how transferable.
Value is earnings after a market wage times a multiple. For this practice that is about $170,000 times roughly 3, cross-checked to about $650,000.
The multiple is held down by one-physician dependence, a falling three-year trend, government fee-for-service payers and untested billing patterns.
A clean independent coding audit turns the biggest discount into a selling point.
Most of what raises value takes two to three years. Pick the year you want to step back and work backward.
Know the deal terms before the first conversation: asset sale, cash-free and debt-free, escrow, non-compete, enrollment.
